  1. Validate inputs.
  2. Set safe execution behavior where appropriate.
  3. Call focused tools.
  4. Check failures explicitly.
  5. Keep data handling simple.
  6. Quote values carefully.
  7. Leave complicated logic to a more suitable language.

  This is less glamorous than treating shell scripting as a clever puzzle, but it reflects
  decades of hard-earned Unix experience.

  ## Conclusion

  The history of Unix shells is the history of an interface becoming a language, then becoming
  a culture. The Thompson shell established command execution and redirection. Pipes turned
  separate utilities into a composable system. The Bourne shell made shell scripting a durable
  programming practice. C shell prioritized interactive convenience. KornShell sought a
  synthesis. POSIX defined a portable common ground. Bash brought a powerful free shell to GNU
  and Linux systems. Zsh and Fish reimagined what an interactive command line could feel like.

  All of these shells share a central Unix insight: useful software does not need to be
  monolithic. Small programs can be connected, redirected, and orchestrated into larger
  workflows. The shell is the place where that composition becomes immediate and human-
  readable.

  Its syntax can be quirky, its historical baggage is real, and its limitations are well
  known. But a Unix shell remains one of computing’s most durable ideas: a compact language
  for telling a machine how existing tools should work together.
